title: Gyárfás–Sumner Conjecture
statement_text: For every forest $F$ and every integer $k \geq 0$, every graph $G$ with $\omega(G) \leq k$ and $\chi(G)$ sufficiently large contains $F$ as an induced subgraph.
context_text: The paper notes that if $G$ has bounded clique number and very large chromatic number, no graph $H$ with a cycle can be a guaranteed induced subgraph (since $G$ can have arbitrarily large girth), but Gyárfás [9] and Sumner [20] conjectured that every forest does appear. The authors note they have nothing new to say about it in general, but prove it for string graphs as a consequence of their main results.
paper_contribution: The paper inadvertently proves the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture for string graphs: since every tree is a tree of lamps, and the main result (1.9) shows every tree of lamps appears as an induced subgraph in every string graph with bounded clique number and sufficiently large chromatic number (using $\mu = 3$ so that $K^1_{3,3}$ is excluded), the conjecture holds for the class of all string graphs.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. V. Chandeliers and strings

title: Conjecture: every forest of lanterns is pervasive
statement_text: Every forest of lanterns $H$ is pervasive; that is, for all $\nu, \ell \geq 0$ there exists $c$ such that every graph $G$ with $\omega(G) \leq \nu$ and $\chi(G) > c$ contains an induced subgraph isomorphic to an $(\geq \ell)$-subdivision of $H$.
context_text: A subdivision of $H$ is obtained by replacing each edge $uv$ by a path joining $u,v$, these paths being internally disjoint; it is an $(\geq \ell)$-subdivision if each of these paths has at least $\ell+1$ edges. $\omega(G)$ is the clique number. A graph $H$ is pervasive in an ideal $\mathcal{C}$ (a class closed under isomorphism and induced subgraphs) if for all $\nu,\ell\geq 0$ there is $c$ such that every $G\in\mathcal{C}$ with $\omega(G)\le\nu$ and $\chi(G)>c$ contains an induced $(\geq\ell)$-subdivision of $H$; pervasive means pervasive in the class of all graphs. Let $T$ be a tree with at least two vertices and add a new vertex $v$ adjacent to every leaf of $T$ (and possibly to some other vertices of $T$): the result is a lantern with pivot $v$ (the one- and two-vertex complete graphs also count as lanterns). A tree of lanterns is built by starting from a lantern and repeatedly taking a new lantern and identifying its pivot with some vertex of what has been built so far; a forest of lanterns is a graph whose components are trees of lanterns. All forests and all cycles are known to be pervasive. Combining results of Chalopin, Esperet, Li and Ossona de Mendez on the Burling (Pawlik et al.) graphs, which are triangle-free string graphs of unbounded chromatic number, a graph $H$ has a $(\geq 2)$-subdivision appearing as an induced subgraph in some Burling graph if and only if $H$ is a forest of lanterns; hence every pervasive graph is a forest of lanterns, and the authors suggest that perhaps the converse is true. An ideal is $\rho$-controlled if there is a nondecreasing $\phi$ such that $\chi(H)\le\phi(\chi^{\rho}(H))$ for every induced subgraph $H$ of a graph in the ideal, where $\chi^\rho(H)$ is the maximum chromatic number of a ball of radius $\rho$ in $H$. The paper proves that every forest of lanterns is pervasive in every $\rho$-controlled ideal ($\rho\geq 2$), and in the class of string graphs, but the question for the ideal of all graphs remains open.
notes: Stated as 'perhaps the converse is true' in the introduction and as an explicitly open problem in the abstract; no formal conjecture environment.
paper_title: Induced subgraphs of graphs with large chromatic number. V. Chandeliers and strings
